Measure

Measure and integration theory develops the necessary tool for solving PDEs and stochastic processes.

σ\sigmaσ-Algebra¶

Motivation¶

In physics, the task of finiding “volume” is ubquitous. For instance in computing mass, charge, the integral would resemble:

∫(⋅)dV\int (\cdot ) dV∫(⋅)dV
(1)

In some sense, this dVdVdV is a function dV:E→RdV:E\to \mathbb{R}dV:E→R which computes the volume of E⊂RnE\subset \mathbb{R}^nE⊂Rn, a tiny control volume we are interested in. It would be very natural to ask for this function to satisfy:

Definition 1 (Measure)

Suppose XXX is a set. Let μ:A→R\mu: A \to \mathbb{R}μ:A→R where A∈P(X)A\in P(X)A∈P(X) such that:

  • μ(∅)=0\mu(\varnothing)=0μ(∅)=0
    (2)

  • (countable additivity) E1,E2,....E_1,E_2,....E1​,E2​,.... is a countable inifnite sequence of disjoint, then:

    μ(∪jEj)=∑jμ(Ej)\mu(\cup_j E_j)=\sum_j \mu(E_j)μ(∪j​Ej​)=j∑​μ(Ej​)
    (3)

    Then we call μ\muμ a measure.

The question would be, when can we find such a function. Trivially we can obtain such property by sending every AAA to 0. However, for more practical purposes of modeling the world, we would like nicer properties. In particular, let’s consider this compeletly reasonable demand on Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn.

Construction of Measure¶

The big picture¶

The general idea of constructing measure is, in crude terms:

  1. Find a collection of set that has a clear notion of size

  2. Approximate arbitrary subsets using element in the elementary set, hence get a notion of size on arbtirary subsets

  3. Make the notion of size truely a measure by restricting to a special collection of subset.

Observe how the notion of size ripens:

Stage 1: ∣⋅∣:E→R+⟶Stage 2: μ∗:P(X)→R+⟶Stage 3: μ:M∣μ∗→R+\begin{align*} \text{Stage 1: $\boxed{|\cdot|:\mathcal E \to \mathbb{R}^+}$} &\longrightarrow \text{Stage 2: $\boxed{\mu^* : P(X)\to \mathbb{R}^+}$} \\ &\longrightarrow \text{Stage 3: $\boxed{\mu: \mathcal M|_{\mu^*} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}}$} \end{align*}Stage 1: ∣⋅∣:E→R+​​⟶Stage 2: μ∗:P(X)→R+​⟶Stage 3: μ:M∣μ∗​→R+​​
(12)

  1. Stage 1 to 2: Create a notion of size on arbitrary sets A⊂P(X)A\subset P(X)A⊂P(X) by approximating them using “building blocks”(A∈E)(A\in \mathcal E)(A∈E) which has a notion of size ∣⋅∣|\cdot |∣⋅∣. This scarifices additivity and we instead of countable sub-additivity

  2. Stage 2 to 3: Shrink the domain by restrict to a particular family M∣μ∗⊂P(X)\mathcal M |_{\mu^*}\subset P(X)M∣μ∗​⊂P(X). This gives us countable additivity and μ\muμ is now a complete measure

Example 1

Concretely, think E\mathcal EE as the set of all open rectangles in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2:

E={(a,b)×(c,d)∣a<b,c<d;a,b,c,d∈R}\mathcal E= \{(a,b)\times (c,d) | a<b,c<d; a,b,c,d\in \mathbb{R}\}E={(a,b)×(c,d)∣a<b,c<d;a,b,c,d∈R}
(13)

These clearly “canonical” notion of size, namingly:

∣A∣=(d−c)(b−a)|A|=(d-c)(b-a)∣A∣=(d−c)(b−a)
(14)

Now using these as “building blocks”, we can measure arbitrary sets E∈P(R2)E\in P(\mathbb{R}^2)E∈P(R2), for instance, a unit circle. Here is a quick numerical demo for approximating a unit circle denoted by EEE with squares on a grid. The resolution nnn is defined as the number of intervals in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).

As we take finer and finer squares, we approach a limit(or the liminf). This number can be used as a notion of size for the set EEE. This motivates the definition of outer measure.

How did we compute that?

A simple way is to count grid points that is inside the unit circle. A quick julia implementation gives the above plot:

function compute_area_of_circle(n)
    cover::Int = 0
    for i in -n:n
        for j in -n:n
            if ((i/n)^2 + (j/n)^2) < 1
                if i == 0 && j == 0
                    cover += 4
                elseif i == 0 || j == 0 
                    cover += 2
                else 
                    cover += 1
                end 
            end
        end
    end
    return cover * (1/n)^2
end

Outer Measure¶

So how do we actually construct measures no matter what set we are working on?(Though in this book we are really interested in just Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn). A general guidline is:

  1. Find some elementary set E\mathcal{E}E where premeasure is defined on the disjoint uniont of E\mathcal{E}E.

  2. Define the measure of arbitrary subset A∈P(X)A\in P(X)A∈P(X) as the the size of “smallest” cover of AA A using the elementary set:

inf⁡{∑ν=1∞ρ(Eν):Eν∈E,A⊂⋃ν=1∞Eν}\inf \left\{\sum_{\nu=1}^{\infty} \rho(E_{\nu}): E_{\nu}\in \mathcal{E}, A\subset \bigcup_{\nu=1}^{\infty} E_{\nu}\right\}inf{ν=1∑∞​ρ(Eν​):Eν​∈E,A⊂ν=1⋃∞​Eν​}
(15)

More generally we can define an outer measure as follows:

Definition 2 (Outer Measure)

An outer measure on an non-empty set XXX is a function μ∗:P(X)→[0,∞]\mu^* : P(X)\to [0,\infty]μ∗:P(X)→[0,∞] such that:

  • μ∗(∅)=0\mu^*(\varnothing)=0μ∗(∅)=0

  • If A⊂BA\subset BA⊂B, then μ∗(A)<μ∗(B)\mu^*(A)<\mu^*(B)μ∗(A)<μ∗(B)

  • μ∗(∪νAν)≤∑νμ∗(Aν)\mu^*(\cup_{\nu}A_{\nu})\leq \sum_{\nu} \mu^* (A_{\nu })μ∗(∪ν​Aν​)≤∑ν​μ∗(Aν​)

We note that property (2),(3) are both derived properties of measure. So we can think the definition of outer measure as a relaxation of measure: take out countable additvity and adds back two derived property. In addition, We note that (15) obeys Definition 2

Exercise

Show that (15) indeed defines an outer measure Definition 2.

Carathéodory Family Mμ∗\mathcal M_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​¶

How do we then obtain measure from outer measure? We note that what outer measure lacks is finite additivity, so we can further ask, is there a collection of subset M⊂P(X)\mathcal {M}\subset P(X)M⊂P(X) such that μ∗\mu^*μ∗ is actually finitey additive? The answer is actually YES! However this seems rather arbitrary:

M={A⊂X:μ∗(F)=μ∗(F−A)+μ∗(A∩F),∀F⊂X}\mathcal M = \{A\subset X: \mu^*(F)=\mu^*(F-A)+\mu^*(A\cap F), \forall F \subset X\}M={A⊂X:μ∗(F)=μ∗(F−A)+μ∗(A∩F),∀F⊂X}
(16)

We call elements of M\mathcal MM μ∗\mu^*μ∗-measureable. In plain English, this saying AAA can “split measure” arbitrary F⊂XF\subset XF⊂X by measuring the intersection and the complement separetly and add them together.

Theorem 1 (Carathéodory’s Theorem)

If μ∗\mu^*μ∗ is an outer measure of XXX then

  1. the collection of μ∗\mu^*μ∗-measureable sets:

    M={A⊂X:μ∗(F)=μ∗(Ac∩F)+μ∗(A∩F),∀F⊂X}\mathcal M = \{A\subset X: \mu^*(F)=\mu^*(A^c \cap F)+\mu^*(A\cap F), \forall F \subset X\}M={A⊂X:μ∗(F)=μ∗(Ac∩F)+μ∗(A∩F),∀F⊂X}
    (17)

    is a σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

  2. μ∗∣M\mu^*|_{\mathcal M}μ∗∣M​ is a complete measure

Premeasure and The Extension Theorem¶

THe workflow (12) is already very promising except one key issue:

Carathéodary Family can be Small

What if Mμ∗\mathcal M_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​ is trivial or very samll?

The next theorem prevents this by starting with an algebra A\mathcal AA instead of just a plain family of sets E\mathcal EE. The plain notion of size on E\mathcal EE is replaced by the so-called premeasure.

Definition 3 (Premeasure)

Suppose A⊂P(X)\mathcal A\subset \mathcal P(X)A⊂P(X) is an algebra, a function μ0:A→[0,∞]\mu_0 : \mathcal A\to [0,\infty]μ0​:A→[0,∞] is a premeasure if

  1. μ0(∅)=0\mu_0(\varnothing)=0μ0​(∅)=0

  2. Let {Aj}1∞\{A_j\}_1^{\infty}{Aj​}1∞​ is a sequence of disjoint sets in A\mathcal AA. Given ⋃1∞Aj∈A\bigcup_1^{\infty} A_j \in \mathcal A⋃1∞​Aj​∈A then

    μ0(⋃1∞)=∑1∞μ0(Aj)\mu_0 \left( \bigcup_1^{\infty}\right) = \sum_{1}^{\infty} \mu_0(A_j)μ0​(1⋃∞​)=1∑∞​μ0​(Aj​)
    (18)
Exercise 2 (Completeness of Mμ∗\mathcal M_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​[1])

A measure μ\muμ on a σ\sigmaσ-algebra M\mathcal{M}M is complete if

∀N∈M∀N′⊆N(μ(N)=0⇒N′∈M).\forall N \in \mathcal{M} \quad \forall N' \subseteq N \quad (\mu(N) = 0 \Rightarrow N' \in \mathcal{M}).∀N∈M∀N′⊆N(μ(N)=0⇒N′∈M).
(19)

Let μ∗\mu^*μ∗ be an outer measure on a set XXX. Prove that the measure on Mμ∗\mathcal{M}_{\mu^*}Mμ∗​ induced by μ∗\mu^*μ∗ by the Carathéodory construction is complete. (The proof of Carathéodory theorem in the book does not explain this well, write a detailed proof.)

Solution to Exercise 2
Proof 1

Note that μ(N)=0⟹μ(N′)=0\mu(N)=0\Longrightarrow \mu(N')=0μ(N)=0⟹μ(N′)=0. ∀E⊆X\forall E\subseteq X∀E⊆X, by subadditivity:

μ∗(E)≤μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)\mu^*(E) \leq \mu^*(E\cap N') + \mu^*(E\cap N'^c)μ∗(E)≤μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)
(20)

By monotoncity and positivity of μ∗\mu^*μ∗ we have μ∗(E∩N′)=0\mu^*(E\cap N')=0μ∗(E∩N′)=0(since E∩N′⊆N′E\cap N' \subseteq N'E∩N′⊆N′ so μ∗(E∩N′)≤0\mu^*(E\cap N')\leq 0μ∗(E∩N′)≤0). But again by monotonicity μ∗(E∩N′c)≤μ∗(E)\mu^*(E\cap N'^c) \leq \mu^*(E)μ∗(E∩N′c)≤μ∗(E) hence we have:

μ∗(E)≤μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)≤μ∗(E)\mu^*(E) \leq \mu^*(E\cap N') + \mu^*(E\cap N'^c) \leq \mu^*(E)μ∗(E)≤μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)≤μ∗(E)
(21)

Hence:

μ∗(E)=μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)\mu^*(E) = \mu^*(E\cap N') + \mu^*(E\cap N'^c)μ∗(E)=μ∗(E∩N′)+μ∗(E∩N′c)
(22)

As desired.

hence we can find A∈AσA\in A_{\sigma}A∈Aσ​ that correponds to ccc.

Solution to Exercise 4

The following exercise is assumed everywhere in mathematics and is not directly related to outer measure. But they are invokded multiple times, for instance, in subadditivity of outer measure.

Exercise 5 (Order invariance for Series of Positive Terms [1])

  1. Prove that any generalized series with summands in [0,∞][0, \infty][0,∞] can be summed in any order. Specifically, if aj∈[0,∞]a_j \in [0, \infty]aj​∈[0,∞] for j∈N={1,2,3,… }j \in \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}j∈N={1,2,3,…}, then for any bijection N→N, j↦kj\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N},\ j \mapsto k_jN→N, j↦kj​, the equality ∑j=1∞aj=∑j=1∞akj\sum_{j=1}^\infty a_j = \sum_{j=1}^\infty a_{k_j}∑j=1∞​aj​=∑j=1∞​akj​​ holds. (That is, a nonnegative generalized series can be summed in any order.)

  2. Prove that any two generalized series with summands in [0,∞][0, \infty][0,∞] can be summed as one series. Specifically, if aj,bj∈[0,∞]a_j, b_j \in [0, \infty]aj​,bj​∈[0,∞] for j∈Nj \in \mathbb{N}j∈N, then the equality ∑j=1∞aj+∑j=1∞bj=∑j=1∞(aj+bj)\sum_{j=1}^\infty a_j + \sum_{j=1}^\infty b_j = \sum_{j=1}^\infty (a_j + b_j)∑j=1∞​aj​+∑j=1∞​bj​=∑j=1∞​(aj​+bj​) holds.

Solution to Exercise 5

  1. We first make a claim

    ∑j∈Naj=sup⁡J∑j∈Jaj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}}a_j = \sup_J \sum_{j\in J} a_jj∈N∑​aj​=Jsup​j∈J∑​aj​
    (32)

    where J⊂N,∣J∣<∞J\subset \mathbb{N}, |J|<\inftyJ⊂N,∣J∣<∞.

  • To show ∑j∈Naj≤sup⁡∑j∈Jaj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_j \leq \sup \sum_{j\in J} a_j ∑j∈N​aj​≤sup∑j∈J​aj​:

    ∑j∈Naj=lim⁡N→∞∑j=1Naj≤sup⁡∑j∈Jaj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}}a_j=\lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{j=1}^N a_j \leq \sup \sum_{j\in J} a_jj∈N∑​aj​=N→∞lim​j=1∑N​aj​≤supj∈J∑​aj​
    (33)

  • To show ∑j∈Naj≥sup⁡∑j∈Jaj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_j \geq \sup \sum_{j\in J} a_j ∑j∈N​aj​≥sup∑j∈J​aj​, we first note ∀J\forall J∀J as above:

    ∑j∈Naj=sup⁡msm≥smax⁡J≥∑j∈Jaj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_j = \sup_m s_m \geq s_{\max J} \geq \sum_{j\in J} a_jj∈N∑​aj​=msup​sm​≥smaxJ​≥j∈J∑​aj​
    (34)

    Now sup⁡\supsup perserves non-strict inequality so we can take sup⁡\supsup on both sides to get:

    sup⁡J∑j∈Naj=∑j∈Naj≥sup⁡J∑j∈Jaj\sup_{J} \sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_j = \sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_j \geq \sup_J \sum_{j\in J} a_jJsup​j∈N∑​aj​=j∈N∑​aj​≥Jsup​j∈J∑​aj​
    (35)

    as desired. Now (1) becomes trivial since ∀J\forall J∀J defined as above, suppose we define:

    k(J)={k(j):j∈J}k(J)=\{k(j): j\in J\}k(J)={k(j):j∈J}
    (36)

    now by the claim

    ∑j∈Nak(j)=sup⁡J∑j∈J′aj=sup⁡J∑j∈k(J)aj\sum_{j\in \mathbb{N}} a_{k(j)} = \sup_{J} \sum_{j\in J'} a_j = \sup_{J} \sum_{j\in k(J)} a_jj∈N∑​ak(j)​=Jsup​j∈J′∑​aj​=Jsup​j∈k(J)∑​aj​
    (37)

    where the last equality follows as J′J'J′ is also in the set {J⊂N:∣J∣<∞}\{J\subset N: |J|<\infty\}{J⊂N:∣J∣<∞}.

Casestudy: Lebesgue-Stieltjes Measure¶

The most useful set that we would like to equip a measure with is, unarguably, the real numbers R\mathbb{R}R.

Starting Point: The half-intervals¶

Recall that we would start with an elementary collection that has a clear notion of size. We define the h-intervals:

H={(a,b]:a<b,a,b∈R}H=\{(a,b]:a<b, a,b\in \mathbb{R}\}H={(a,b]:a<b,a,b∈R}
(39)

We define a terminology here:

Definition 4 (Borel Sets)

Let XXX any metric space, the σ\sigmaσ-algebra genereated by the family of open sets in XXX is called the Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra, denoted by BX\mathcal B_{X}BX​

Exercise 6 (h-intervals generate BR\mathcal B_{\mathbb{R}}BR​)

Check HHH is an elementary set and so it generates an algebra A\mathcal AA. Furthermore, show that the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by A\mathcal AA is BR\mathcal B_{\mathbb{R}}BR​

Another terminology:

Definition 5 (Elementary Decomposition)

Suppose A∈AA\in \mathcal AA∈A, since A=M(H)\mathcal A=\mathcal M(H)A=M(H) we can find finite disjoint h-intervals {Ij}j=1N={(aj,bj]j}j=1N\{I_j\}_{j=1}^N=\{(a_j,b_j]_j\}_{j=1}^N{Ij​}j=1N​={(aj​,bj​]j​}j=1N​ such that:

A=⋃j=1NIjA=\bigcup_{j=1}^N I_jA=j=1⋃N​Ij​
(40)

Then {Ij}\{I_j\}{Ij​} is an elementary decomposition of AAA.

We define size on HHH as follows:

Notion of Size on h-intervals

Let F:R→RF:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}F:R→R be increasing and right-continous, let (a,b]∈H(a,b]\in H(a,b]∈H, then:

∣(a,b]∣=F(b)−F(a)|(a,b]|=F(b)-F(a)∣(a,b]∣=F(b)−F(a)
(41)

Note when F(x)=xF(x)=xF(x)=x, we get the common notion of length of interval.

The next step is to extend this notion of size to A=M(H)\mathcal A=\mathcal M(H)A=M(H).

Step 1: Construction of a premeasure¶

Now we have an algebra A\mathcal AA where elements of the algebra A∈AA\in \mathcal AA∈A has an elementary decomposition A={Ij}A=\{I_j\}A={Ij​} to h-intervals I=(aj,bj]I=(a_j,b_j]I=(aj​,bj​], which is equipped with a notion of size bj−ajb_j-a_jbj​−aj​. A natural way to define the notion of size for AAA is hence:

μ0(A)=∑j=1N∣Ij∣=∑j=1NF(bj)−F(aj)\mu_0(A) = \sum_{j=1}^N |I_j| =\sum_{j=1}^N F(b_j)-F(a_j)μ0​(A)=j=1∑N​∣Ij​∣=j=1∑N​F(bj​)−F(aj​)
(42)

We claim that μ0\mu_0μ0​ is actually a pre-measure on A\mathcal AA.

Proposition 1

Let F:R→RF:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}F:R→R to be a right-continuous, increasing function. Define μ0\mu_0μ0​ as

μ0:A→R⋃j=1NA↦∑j=1N[F(bj)−F(aj)]\begin{align*} \mu_0 : \mathcal A &\to \mathbb{R} \\ \bigcup_{j=1}^N A &\mapsto \sum_{j=1}^N [F(b_j)-F(a_j)] \end{align*}μ0​:Aj=1⋃N​A​→R↦j=1∑N​[F(bj​)−F(aj​)]​
(43)

where {Ij}={(aj,bj]}\{I_j\}=\{(a_j,b_j]\}{Ij​}={(aj​,bj​]} is an elementary decomposition. Then μ0\mu_0μ0​ is a premeasure on A\mathcal AA.

Proof 2 (μ0\mu_0μ0​ is a pre-measure)

We first need to show that μ0\mu_0μ0​ is actually well-defined[2]. Then we illustrate:

  1. Empty set has zero measure

  2. Non-negativity

  3. Finite additivity

  4. Countable additivity where only (1),(2),(4)(1),(2),(4)(1),(2),(4) is truely required. But (3)(3)(3) is used in the proof of (4)(4)(4).

Footnotes¶

  1. This problem is selected from Professor Igor Mineyev’s homework from MATH 540(Real Analysis) in Fall 2026 at UIUC.

  2. Note that in definiting a notion of size μ0\mu_0μ0​ on A∈AA\in \mathcal AA∈A, we requires AAA to have a concrete representation ∪jIj\cup_j I_j∪j​Ij​. If the result is independent on how we choose this representation(i.e. different elementary decomposition{Ij}\{I_j\}{Ij​}), then this notion of size is indeed fundamentally correct. Otherwise if μ0\mu_0μ0​ is dependent on how we choose representation, then it is not a credibe notion of size. Such “representational invariance” is called well-definedness in mathematics.
